assignmentHtml.task:
深入研究 Druid 的迟到事件处理和多租户隔离。调查：

  1. Druid 如何通过 timestampSpec 和 maxFutureIntervalSecs 处理迟到事件？数据段粒度会发生什么变化？
  2. Druid 的“恰好一次”Kafka 摄取——它如何提交偏移量，摄取期间协调器发生故障时会怎样？
  3. Druid 多租户隔离——每个租户一个数据源与使用 tenant_id 的共享数据源的比较；能否防止一个租户耗尽另一个租户的资源？查询优先级？专用 broker？
  4. Druid 恢复操作实际上会恢复什么？Export-metadata 工具只导出 5 张元数据表。必须单独保存深层存储中的数据段文件。如果深层存储丢失，会发生什么？
  5. Druid 复制——没有内置复制；数据段只有单份副本。恢复依赖于从深层存储重新下载。调查 Druid 中“复制因子”的概念。
  6. Druid 版本依据——哪个版本引入了 MSQ（多阶段查询）？
assignmentHtml.context: 证据截止日期为 2026-09-16。工作负载 A：包含迟到事件的点击流、仪表板。工作负载 D：2000 个商家需要隔离。工作负载 F：恢复和回滚语义。Druid 是候选系统。
assignmentHtml.expected_output: 提供深入的 Druid 调研档案，涵盖迟到事件、恰好一次摄取、多租户隔离、恢复语义、复制、版本依据，并附来源 URL。

answerHtml:
COMPREHENSIVE DRUID DOSSIER — Late events, exactly-once ingestion, multi-tenant isolation, restore semantics, replication, and version anchors.

1. LATE EVENT HANDLING

Two ingestion families behave very differently:

A) Stream-pull (Tranquility) realtime ingestion:

  • Uses windowPeriod in tuningConfig (e.g. "PT10M"). Only events within windowPeriod of current time are accepted; events outside the window are rejected (metric: ingest/events/thrownAway). Late/out-of-band events are dropped, not buffered. Batch ingestion is recommended for historical data. [Ingestion FAQ]

B) Kafka indexing service (supervised streaming):

  • Has NO window-period restriction — can ingest arbitrarily old timestamps. This was a major design change vs. stream-pull. [Imply blog: Exactly-Once Streaming Ingestion]
  • Late messages handled via lateMessageRejectionPeriod (reject messages with timestamps earlier than this period before task creation; e.g. PT1H with task at 12:00Z drops messages before 11:00Z) and earlyMessageRejectionPeriod (reject messages later than this period after task reached taskDuration). Mutually exclusive with lateMessageRejectionStartDateTime (absolute alternative). [Supervisor ref]
  • Within a Kafka partition, strict ordering is enforced: every message is verified to follow sequentially in offset order before being parsed/indexed. [Imply blog]
  • Offset handoff consistency check: when publishing, if the segment's starting offsets don't match the last published segment's ending offsets, the segment is rejected (prevents gaps/duplicates). [Storage overview; Imply blog]

Segment granularity behavior:

  • A Kafka indexing task writes consumed events into segments per the configured segmentGranularity (e.g. HOUR). A task keeps writing into the current interval's segment until hitting maxRowsPerSegment, maxTotalRows, or intermediateHandoffPeriod, then creates a new segment for the next interval. [Kafka ingestion doc]
  • Late events falling within an already-passed but still-active interval are absorbed into that interval's segment (the task is still reading/creating segments for that interval). Small/split segments can result when task handoffs straddle interval boundaries (e.g. 4-hour task with hourly granularity); scheduled re-indexing merges them. [Kafka ingestion doc]
  • All segments in the same time chunk must share the same granularity; WEEK granularity is discouraged. [Ingestion spec ref]

2. EXACTLY-ONCE KAFKA INGESTION

Offset commit mechanism:

  • Druid commits stream offsets to its metadata store ALONGSIDE segment metadata, in the SAME database transaction. This atomicity is the core exactly-once guarantee. [Storage overview]
  • The supervisor/publishing task performs a consistency check when writing the offset marker: the segment's starting offsets must equal the ending offsets of the last published segment; otherwise the segment is rejected. Partially-ingested data is discarded; Druid resumes from the last committed offsets. [Storage overview; Imply blog]
  • Supervisors track the latest persisted Kafka offsets in the metadata store so subsequent tasks start reading exactly where previous tasks ended. [Kafka supervisor operations]

Coordinator (Overlord) failure during ingestion:

  • Supervisor specs are persisted in the metadata database. When a new Overlord gains leadership (startup or failover), it spawns a supervisor for each spec in the metadata DB, discovers running Kafka indexing tasks, and attempts to adopt them if compatible with the supervisor's configuration. Incompatible tasks are killed and recreated. Supervisors are thus persistent across Overlord restarts/failovers. [Kafka supervisor operations; Kafka ingestion doc]
  • If expected starting offsets are no longer available in Kafka (retention expired, topic deleted/recreated), the supervisor refuses to start and in-flight tasks fail. Manual reset clears stored offsets (may cause duplicates/skips). [Kafka supervisor operations]
  • Note: Druid does NOT use Kafka consumer-group offset commits for this — offsets live in Druid's own metadata store. Druid reads with isolation.level=read_committed by default (only committed Kafka transactions visible). [Kafka ingestion doc]

3. MULTI-TENANT ISOLATION (2000 MERCHANTS)

Datasource-per-tenant:

  • Pros: independent schema, backfills, partitioning, loading/expiration rules per tenant; faster queries (fewer segments examined per tenant). Cons: each datasource needs its own JVMs for realtime indexing and its own segment files on disk — wasteful at 2000 tenants. [Multitenancy considerations]
  • Compromise: fewer datasources than tenants (e.g., partition tenants across N datasources).

Shared datasource with tenant_id:

  • Most tenants share one datasource with a tenant_id dimension. Partition by tenant_id: multi-dimension range partitioning (batch) or Kafka topic partitioning by hash of tenant_id (realtime). Queries filter on tenant_id. [Multitenancy considerations]

Resource isolation mechanisms (can you prevent one tenant from exhausting another's?): YES, via layered controls:

  • Query priority: priority flag in query context; higher priority gets precedence for computational resources. [Multitenancy considerations]
  • Query laning: reserves Broker HTTP threads for high-priority queries; low-priority queries restricted to general lanes. Config: druid.query.scheduler.laning.strategy (hilo/manual), druid.query.scheduler.numThreads, druid.query.scheduler.laning.maxLowPercent. [Mixed workloads]
  • Service tiering: separate Historical + Broker tiers (hot/cold). Heavy reporting queries routed to cold Brokers; interactive queries to hot Brokers. Historical tiering via load rules (tieredReplicants), druid.server.tier, druid.server.priority. Broker tiering via druid.service=druid:broker-hot. [Mixed workloads]
  • Dedicated brokers per tenant: Router routes queries to tenant-specific Broker pools. Strategies: manual (brokerService from query context) or JavaScript (arbitrary logic). Strict isolation via druid.broker.segment.watchedTiers (Broker only sees specific tiers). SQL routing enabled with druid.router.sql.enable=true. [Router doc; Multitenancy considerations]
  • Caveat: no hard per-tenant CPU/mem quota exists; isolation is achieved architecturally (dedicated pools), not via quotas.

4. RESTORE SEMANTICS

What the export-metadata tool exports (exactly 5 tables):

  • segments, rules, config, datasource, supervisors. These contain: segment metadata payloads (including loadSpec pointing into deep storage), load/retention rules, runtime config, datasource definitions, supervisor specs. [Export-metadata tool]
  • Import targets: Derby, MySQL, PostgreSQL (table-specific COPY/LOAD DATA commands). [Export-metadata tool]
  • Tool limitations: Derby source only; deep-storage rewrites only from local deep storage. Directory structure of segment files must be preserved unchanged (except HDFS colon→underscore renaming). [Export-metadata tool]

What a restore does NOT restore:

  • Segment data files in deep storage are NOT part of the export. They must be preserved separately (S3/HDFS/NFS backups). [Deep storage doc; Export-metadata tool]
  • Task-related tables and audit tables are not exported. [Metadata storage doc]

If deep storage is lost:

  • Data is PERMANENTLY LOST. Deep storage defines durability: "As long as Druid processes can see this storage infrastructure... you will not lose data no matter how many Druid nodes you lose. If segments disappear from this storage layer, then you will lose whatever data those segments represented." [Deep storage doc]
  • Even intact metadata cannot compensate — the metadata only points to segment files; without the files, segments cannot be loaded or queried. The only recovery path is replaying upstream sources (e.g., Kafka topic from the lost segment's start offset). [Perun engineering; Storage overview]
  • Similarly, metadata-store loss is described as having "no way to restore lost metadata" — HA is the recommended mitigation. [Metadata storage doc]

Note: segments marked unused (via kill task / retention) remain recoverable until actually removed by coordinator kill task (disabled by default; when enabled, default 90-day retention). Recovery: "Mark as Used all segments" action re-triggers coordinator loading from deep storage. [Imply blog: Recovering Dropped Segments]

5. REPLICATION

Druid has NO built-in data-level replication (no HDFS-style block replication). Deep storage holds single copies of segment files. [Deep storage doc]

The "replication factor" concept in Druid refers to the number of Historical-tier COPIES of a segment:

  • Configured via load rules' tieredReplicants property: map of tier name → number of replicas (e.g. {"hot": 1, "_default_tier": 1} = 2 total copies). Default when useDefaultTierForNull=true: {"_default_tier": 2}. Must be 0 or positive integer. [Rule configuration]
  • replication_factor in sys.segments shows the configured replica count; 0 means segment exists ONLY in deep storage and is queryable via MSQ from deep storage. [Query from deep storage]
  • Coordinator ensures segments are loaded on N Historical nodes per the configured replication factor; it also rebalances segments across nodes. [Coordinator doc]
  • Failure behavior: if more Historicals go offline than replication factor permits, queries silently return PARTIAL results (no error, missing data). Single-replica setups are especially risky — brokers get "segment not available" and exclude that data. Recommendation: replication factor ≥ 2 for all historical tiers. [Perun engineering]
  • Recovery relies on deep-storage re-download: unavailable segments are reloaded onto other Historicals from deep storage in the background. New nodes also download segments from deep storage. [Storage overview; Deep storage doc]
  • Changing replication factor triggers bulk re-copying from deep storage (I/O storm on Historicals); stage during off-peak, throttle with loadqueuepeon.batchSize. [Perun engineering]

6. VERSION ANCHOR — MSQ (MULTI-STAGE QUERY)

  • MSQ introduced as an EXTENSION in Apache Druid 24.0 (released September 16, 2022). Initial capability: SQL-based batch ingestion (INSERT/REPLACE statements executed as batch tasks on Middle Managers). [Imply blog; Upgrade notes; MSQ docs]
  • Expanded across 25–33 (empty ingest queries, ARRAY columns, etc.). [Upgrade notes]
  • In Druid 35.0.0, MSQ became a CORE capability (removed from druid-multi-stage-query extension; extension ignored/not found in future versions). [Upgrade notes]
  • Query-from-deep-storage (Druid 27+) runs on the MSQ task engine via POST /druid/v2/sql/statements with executionMode=ASYNC. [Query from deep storage]

WORKLOAD FIT SUMMARY:

  • Workload A (clickstream, late events, dashboards): Kafka indexing service handles late events without window restrictions; near-real-time availability supports dashboards; query priority/laning protects interactive queries. Small split segments from handoffs may need periodic re-indexing.
  • Workload D (2000 merchants, isolation): datasource-per-tenant is expensive at this scale; shared datasource with tenant_id + hash-partitioned Kafka topics is the pragmatic choice, with Router-based dedicated broker pools per merchant group and query laning for cross-tenant QoS protection.
  • Workload F (recovery/rollback): Druid's durability model puts data in deep storage (single copy); restore requires both metadata import AND deep storage file preservation. No automatic segment replication — replication factor applies only to Historical-tier copies, not deep storage. Rollback of ingestion errors possible via segment version management and kill-task/unused-segment reactivation within the kill retention window.

evidence.snippet: Druid realtime ingestion only accepts events within a configurable windowPeriod of the current time... Druid will reject events outside of a window period. The best way to see if events are being rejected is to check the Druid ingest metrics.
evidence.supports: Stream-pull realtime ingestion drops late events beyond windowPeriod; metrics ingest/events/thrownAway track rejections

evidence.snippet: The Kafka indexing task is the first real-time ingestion option in Druid that does not require events to fall within a window period... With the removal of the window period restriction, the Kafka indexing service can be used to ingest data with arbitrarily old timestamps... During reading, every message received is verified to ensure that it follows in sequence from the previously received message... if the starting offsets of the to-be-published segment match the ending offsets of the last published segment then the transaction succeeds; otherwise the segment is rejected.
evidence.supports: Kafka indexing has no window restriction; sequential offset verification enforces ordering; publish-time offset consistency check provides exactly-once semantics

evidence.snippet: lateMessageRejectionPeriod: Configures tasks to reject messages with timestamps earlier than this period before the task was created... earlyMessageRejectionPeriod: Configures tasks to reject messages with timestamps later than this period after the task reached its task duration.
evidence.supports: Kafka supervisor config knobs for rejecting late and early messages relative to task creation and taskDuration

evidence.snippet: With these methods, Druid commits stream offsets to its metadata store alongside segment metadata, in the same transaction... partially-ingested data is discarded, and Druid will resume ingestion from the last committed set of stream offsets. This ensures exactly-once publishing behavior.
evidence.supports: Atomic offset+metadata commit in metadata store is the exact mechanism for exactly-once; failure rolls back to last committed offsets

evidence.snippet: When an Overlord gains leadership, either by being started or as a result of another Overlord failing, it will spawn a supervisor for each supervisor spec in the metadata database. The supervisor will then discover running Kafka indexing tasks and will attempt to adopt them if they are compatible... In this way, the supervisors are persistent across Overlord restarts and fail-overs.
evidence.supports: Coordinator/Overlord failure: supervisors resume from metadata DB, adopt running tasks; incompatible tasks killed and recreated

evidence.snippet: The indexing service keeps track of the latest persisted Kafka offsets in order to provide exactly-once ingestion guarantees across tasks. Subsequent tasks must start reading from where the previous task completed in order for the generated segments to be accepted. If the messages at the expected starting offsets are no longer available in Kafka... the supervisor will refuse to start and in flight tasks will fail.
evidence.supports: Persisted offset tracking across tasks; offset unavailability causes supervisor refusal requiring manual reset

evidence.snippet: Multitenant workloads can either use a separate datasource for each tenant, or can share one or more datasources between tenants using a 'tenant_id' dimension... Each datasource requires its own JVMs for realtime indexing... Druid queries can optionally set a priority flag in the query context reference... Broker processes can also be dedicated to a given tier... Druid also provides a Router process that can route queries to different Brokers based on various query parameters (datasource, interval, etc.).
evidence.supports: Both isolation patterns documented; query priority, dedicated brokers, and Router-based routing for resource isolation

evidence.snippet: Query lanes are analogous to carpool and normal lanes... Druid restricts low priority queries to the general lanes and allows high priority queries to run wherever possible... druid.query.scheduler.laning.strategy... druid.query.scheduler.numThreads... druid.query.scheduler.laning.maxLowPercent... Service tiering: define separate groups of Historicals and Brokers... assign Brokers to tiers via druid.service=druid:broker-hot... druid.broker.segment.watchedTiers restricts a Broker to only see segments on specific tiers. This provides strict query isolation.
evidence.supports: Query laning (thread reservation), service tiering (separate Historical+Broker tiers), and watchedTiers for strict tenant/workload isolation

evidence.snippet: The Router service distributes queries between different Broker services... manual strategy reads the parameter brokerService from the query context and routes the query to that broker service... JavaScript strategy allows defining arbitrary routing rules... druid.router.tierToBrokerMap maps tier to broker service.
evidence.supports: Router enables dedicated broker pools per tenant via manual/JS routing strategies and tier-to-broker mapping

evidence.snippet: This tool exports the contents of the following Druid metadata tables: segments, rules, config, datasource, supervisors... The <table-name>.csv files are used for import into another database such as MySQL and PostgreSQL... For deep storage migration, the rewrite performed by this tool requires that the directory structure of the segments be unchanged.
evidence.supports: Export-metadata exports exactly 5 metadata tables; segment files must be copied separately with identical structure; tool only rewrites pointers

evidence.snippet: Deep storage is where segments are stored. It is a storage mechanism that Apache Druid does not provide. This deep storage infrastructure defines the level of durability of your data. As long as Druid processes can see this storage infrastructure and get at the segments stored on it, you will not lose data no matter how many Druid nodes you lose. If segments disappear from this storage layer, then you will lose whatever data those segments represented.
evidence.supports: Deep storage is the durability boundary; single copies; data loss if deep storage files disappear

evidence.snippet: We also recommend you set up a high availability environment because there is no way to restore lost metadata.
evidence.supports: Metadata loss is irrecoverable; HA is the only mitigation

evidence.snippet: tieredReplicants: Map from tier names to the respective number of segment replicas to be loaded on those tiers. The number of replicas for each tier must be either 0 or a positive integer. Default when useDefaultTierForNull is true: {'_default_tier': 2}.
evidence.supports: Replication factor in Druid = Historical-tier replica count configured via tieredReplicants; default 2 copies on _default_tier

evidence.snippet: Segments with a replication_factor of 0 are not assigned to any Historical tiers. Queries against these segments are run directly against the segment in deep storage.
evidence.supports: replication_factor=0 means deep-storage-only segments; queryable via MSQ from deep storage

evidence.snippet: Mitigation requires setting segment replication factor to at least 2 for all historical tiers... if the segment has only one replica... the broker receives a segment not available response and returns results that exclude the data covered by that segment... Druid brokers do not return an error when segments are unavailable — they return partial results with no indication that data is missing.
evidence.supports: Single-replica setups silently return incomplete results; replication factor >= 2 recommended; no replication at deep-storage level

evidence.snippet: Apache Druid 24.0 contains over 324 updates... A multi-stage query (MSQ) task engine... enables you to transform and ingest batch data in Druid using SQL.
evidence.supports: MSQ first introduced as extension in Druid 24.0 (Sep 16, 2022)

evidence.snippet: Multi-stage query task engine: The MSQ task engine is now a core capability of Druid rather than an extension. It has been in the default extension load list for several releases.
evidence.supports: MSQ became core capability in Druid 35.0.0; was extension prior

evidence.snippet: Druid assigns Kafka partitions to each Kafka indexing task. A task writes the events it consumes from Kafka into a single segment for the segment granularity interval until it reaches one of the following limits: maxRowsPerSegment, maxTotalRows, or intermediateHandoffPeriod. At this point, the task creates a new partition for this segment granularity to contain subsequent events.
evidence.supports: Kafka indexing writes per-segment-granularity intervals; late events within active interval merge into existing segment; split segments can occur at task handoff boundaries

evidence.snippet: segmentGranularity: Time chunking granularity for this datasource... Note that all segments in the same time chunk should have the same segment granularity. Avoid WEEK granularity... queryGranularity: The resolution of timestamp storage within each segment. This must be equal to, or finer, than segmentGranularity.
evidence.supports: Granularity constraints: uniform within time chunk; queryGranularity must be <= segmentGranularity
